meta.case_name: Reducing Wait Times at the Ski Station

prompt.context: The manager of a ski field has hired you to analyze how the time that skiers spend in the queue can be reduced. There are two options: increase the speed of the ski lift or build another equal lift. There are no budget constraints in the decision. The ski field, with one lift and one slope, has a limit of 200 skiers and is full every day. The lift has a speed of 5 skiers per minute and it takes 10 minutes for the lift to carry a skier to the top of the slope. Skiers take 5 minutes on average to ski down and get in the queue again.
prompt.question: Which of the two options would you recommend the manager pursue in order to reduce the time skiers spend waiting in the queue?

clarifying_info.q: Can the mountain accommodate more skiers if a second lift is built?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — with two lifts the mountain can hold double the number of skiers (400 skiers), though the current limit remains 200.

framework: Step 1: Calculate the current queue time under baseline conditions (1 lift, 200 skiers, lift speed 5/min, lift time 10 min, ski-down time 5 min)
Step 2: Analyze Option A — increase lift speed (e.g., halve lift transit time to 5 min) and recalculate queue time
Step 3: Analyze Option B — add a second identical lift and recalculate queue time
Step 4: Compare queue times across all three scenarios and recommend the superior option

questions.prompt: What is the current (baseline) queue time with one lift?
questions.guidance: Use the flow-balance equation: at steady state, all 200 skiers are distributed across three phases — on the lift, skiing down, or in the queue. Skiers on lift = lift speed x lift time = 5 x 10 = 50. Skiers skiing down = lift speed x ski-down time = 5 x 5 = 25. Skiers in queue = 200 - 50 - 25 = 125. Queue time = skiers in queue / lift speed = 125 / 5 = 25 minutes. Alternatively use the cycle-time formula: Ski_lift_speed x (Min_queue + Min_lift + Min_skiing) = Total_skiers / # lifts → 5 x (Q + 10 + 5) = 200/1 → Q = 40 - 15 = 25 min.

math.setup: Method 1 (flow balance): Skiers_on_lift = 5 x 10 = 50; Skiers_skiing = 5 x 5 = 25; Skiers_in_queue = 200 - 50 - 25 = 125; Queue_time = 125 / 5

questions.prompt: Option A: If the lift speed is increased to halve transit time (lift time becomes 5 minutes), what is the new queue time?
questions.guidance: With faster lift, the lift carries skiers to the top in 5 min instead of 10. Recalculate with lift time = 5 min. Method 1: Skiers on lift = 5 x 5 = 25; Skiers skiing = 5 x 5 = 25; Skiers in queue = 200 - 25 - 25 = 150; Queue time = 150 / 5 = 30 min. Paradoxically queue time INCREASES because the lift empties faster, creating a larger pool waiting. Method 2: 5 x (Q + 5 + 5) = 200 → Q = 40 - 10 = 30 min. The interviewee may use a different assumption for speed increase (the conclusion must remain the same — Option A is worse).

math.setup: Lift time reduced to 5 min; all other parameters unchanged
steps: Check via cycle formula: 5 × (Q + 5 + 5) = 200 → Q = 30 min
math.answer: 30 minutes (queue time INCREASES — Option A is counterproductive)

questions.prompt: Option B: If a second identical lift is built, what is the new queue time?
questions.guidance: Two lifts together carry 2 x 5 = 10 skiers/min. Skiers on both lifts = 10 x 10 = 100; Skiers skiing = 10 x 5 = 50; Skiers in queue = 200 - 100 - 50 = 50; Queue time = 50 / 10 = 5 min. Method 2: combined capacity means (50/2) / 5 = 25 skier-minutes per lift → queue time 5 min. The cycle formula: 5 x (Q + 10 + 5) = 200 / 2 lifts → each lift serves 100 skiers → 5Q = 100 - 75 = 25 → Q = 5 min.

math.setup: Two lifts, each with speed 5 skiers/min and transit time 10 min; 200 skiers total
steps: Note: casebook also expresses as (50/2) / 5 = 5 min per-lift basis
math.answer: 5 minutes (queue time drops from 25 to 5 min)

brainstorming.prompt: What other measures could the manager take to reduce queue time beyond the two options analyzed?

categories.name: Slope/infrastructure changes
ideas: Lengthen or widen the ski run to increase ski-down time, reducing the fraction of time skiers spend in the queue
Build additional slopes to distribute skier traffic

categories.name: Demand management
ideas: Increase ticket prices to reduce skier volume during peak periods
Introduce timed entry slots or advance reservations
Offer off-peak discounts to redistribute demand

categories.name: Queue experience and throughput
ideas: Build a cafeteria or rest area mid-mountain to absorb skiers out of the queue
Use a reservation or virtual-queue system so skiers can wait elsewhere
Train lift operators to board skiers faster

categories.name: Operational adjustments
ideas: Extend operating hours to spread 200 skiers across more time
Run a separate beginner-only lift or area to segment traffic

recommendation: Build a second identical lift (Option B). This reduces queue time from 25 minutes to 5 minutes — an 80% reduction.
Increasing lift speed (Option A) is counterproductive: halving transit time raises queue time from 25 to 30 minutes because skiers circulate faster but the single lift remains the bottleneck.
risks: Capital cost of a second lift, though the problem states there are no budget constraints
Additional capacity (second lift can handle 400 skiers) may incentivize overcrowding if the skier limit is raised without corresponding slope capacity
Operational complexity of running two lifts simultaneously
next_steps: Confirm mountain slope capacity can support higher throughput if the skier limit is eventually raised
Evaluate complementary demand-management measures (pricing, reservations) to optimize the skier experience year-round
Assess lift maintenance scheduling to ensure both lifts can run simultaneously during peak season
